In the shadow of wooded hills near the confluence of the Kentucky and Ohio rivers is Lanes Landing, the 125-acre farm where Wendell Berry tended the land and published the most trenchant appeals in American letters to tame the damage from industrial agriculture. “No amount of fiddling with capitalism to regulate and humanize it can, for long, disguise its failure to conserve the wealth and health of nature, eroded, wasted, or degraded soils, damaged or destroyed ecosystems, extinction of biodiversity species,” he wrote. “Whole landscapes defaced, gouged, flooded, or blown up – thoughtless squandering of fossil fuels and fossil waters, of mineable minerals and ores, natural health and beauty replaced by a heartless and sickening ugliness.” A man who plowed with draft horses and wrote with pencils on yellow legal pads, Berry died on August 31, at age 92, in Port Royal, Kentucky. He had spent half a century there composing classic poems, lyrical essays, and landmark books that illustrate and attack the depredations of contemporary industrialized farm practices. Water pollution was but one argument in the wholesale indictment. He wasn’t the first writer to view the ever-larger scale of mechanization in agriculture as an affront to human and ecological safety. In 1940, in An Agricultural Testament, a foundational book that launched the modern organic farming movement, Sir Albert Howard wrote, “Mother Earth never attempts to farm without livestock; she always raises mixed crops; great pains are taken to preserve the soil and to prevent erosion; the mixed vegetable and animal wastes are converted into humus; there is no waste.” Circle of Blue WaterNews Weekly water news delivered directly to your inbox The Stream Global water news delivered twice a week.
